subject.name: Physics
subject.overview: ICSE Class 9 Physics builds the quantitative foundation for Class 10. It starts with measurement using instruments such as vernier callipers, the screw gauge and the simple pendulum, then moves to motion in one dimension, the equations of motion and graphs. Newton's laws, momentum and gravitation follow. Two chapters cover fluids: pressure, Pascal's law, atmospheric pressure, upthrust, Archimedes' principle and floatation. The course also covers heat and energy, including anomalous expansion of water and the greenhouse effect, reflection from plane and spherical mirrors, the propagation of sound, basic current electricity and magnetism. Numerical problem solving with correct SI units runs through most chapters.
studyTips: Write every numerical in three steps: list the given quantities with SI units, write the formula, then substitute and give the answer with its unit.
Practise reading vernier callipers and screw gauge scales, including positive and negative zero errors, until the least count calculation is automatic.
Learn the three equations of motion together with the meaning of slope and area for distance-time and velocity-time graphs.
For fluids, always check whether a question asks for pressure due to the liquid alone or total pressure including atmospheric pressure.
Draw neat ray diagrams and magnetic field line diagrams with arrows, since unlabelled diagrams lose marks.

chapters.name: Measurements and Experimentation
chapters.summary: Covers SI units, the least count of instruments and precise measurement using vernier callipers, the screw gauge and the simple pendulum.

chapters.name: Motion in One Dimension
chapters.summary: Describes motion along a straight line using distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration, the equations of motion and motion graphs.

chapters.name: Laws of Motion
chapters.summary: Introduces inertia, momentum and Newton's three laws of motion, along with Newton's law of gravitation, mass and weight.

topics.name: Newton's third law and conservation of momentum

chapters.name: Pressure in Fluids and Atmospheric Pressure
chapters.summary: Explains thrust and pressure, pressure exerted by liquids at a depth, Pascal's law with the hydraulic press, and atmospheric pressure.

chapters.name: Upthrust in Fluids, Archimedes' Principle and Floatation
chapters.summary: Covers the buoyant force, Archimedes' principle, relative density and the principle of floatation.

chapters.name: Heat and Energy
chapters.summary: Distinguishes heat and temperature, explains the anomalous expansion of water, and discusses energy sources, the greenhouse effect and global warming.

chapters.name: Reflection of Light
chapters.summary: Covers the laws of reflection, images formed by plane mirrors, multiple images in inclined mirrors and basic spherical mirror terms.

chapters.name: Propagation of Sound Waves
chapters.summary: Describes sound as a mechanical longitudinal wave, the terms used for waves, the speed of sound in different media and ultrasound.

topics.name: Speed of sound in different media

chapters.name: Current Electricity
chapters.summary: Introduces electric charge, current, potential difference, resistance, conductors and insulators, and simple circuits.

chapters.name: Magnetism
chapters.summary: Covers properties of magnets, induced magnetism, magnetic field lines and neutral points, and electromagnets.

questions.text: The main scale of a vernier callipers is marked in millimetres and 10 vernier divisions coincide with 9 main scale divisions. The least count is:
questions.answer: 0.1 mm. Least count = 1 MSD − 1 VSD = 1 mm − 0.9 mm = 0.1 mm.
questions.explanation: One vernier division is 9/10 mm, so it is shorter than a main scale division by 0.1 mm.

questions.text: The SI unit of length is the ____.
questions.answer: The SI unit of length is the metre (m).

questions.text: A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale. It has no zero error. While measuring the diameter of a wire, the main scale reading is 3.5 mm and the 22nd circular scale division coincides with the reference line. Find the diameter of the wire in mm.
questions.answer: Least count = pitch / number of circular divisions = 0.5 mm / 50 = 0.01 mm. Diameter = MSR + (CSR × LC) = 3.5 mm + (22 × 0.01 mm) = 3.5 + 0.22 = 3.72 mm.

questions.text: A simple pendulum completes 20 oscillations in 40 s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and π² = 10, find the effective length of the pendulum in metres.
questions.explanation: A pendulum with a time period of 2 s is called a seconds pendulum.

questions.text: What is meant by the zero error of a vernier callipers? How is the correct reading obtained when the instrument has a zero error?
questions.answer: Zero error: when the two jaws of the vernier callipers are closed and the zero of the vernier scale does not coincide with the zero of the main scale, the instrument has a zero error (positive if the vernier zero lies to the right of the main scale zero, negative if to the left). Correction: correct reading = observed reading − zero error, taking the sign of the zero error into account (so a negative zero error is effectively added).

questions.text: The slope of a velocity–time graph gives the:
questions.answer: Acceleration. Slope = change in velocity / time taken, which is acceleration.
questions.explanation: The area under a velocity–time graph gives displacement, not the slope.

questions.text: The area enclosed between a velocity–time graph and the time axis gives the ____ of the body.
questions.answer: The area under a velocity–time graph gives the displacement of the body.

questions.text: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 5 s. Find its final velocity in m/s.
questions.answer: u = 0, a = 2 m/s², t = 5 s. Using v = u + at: v = 0 + 2 × 5 = 10 m/s.

questions.text: A car moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest by applying brakes uniformly. It stops after covering 50 m. Find the magnitude of its retardation in m/s².
questions.answer: u = 20 m/s, v = 0, s = 50 m. Using v² = u² + 2as: 0 = 20² + 2 × a × 50, so 0 = 400 + 100a, giving a = −4 m/s². The retardation is 4 m/s².
questions.explanation: The negative sign of acceleration shows the velocity is decreasing; retardation is its magnitude.

questions.text: A ball is thrown vertically upwards with a speed of 20 m/s from the top of a tower 25 m high. The ball then falls past the tower to the ground. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, find the total time in seconds after which the ball hits the ground.
questions.answer: Take upward as positive, origin at the top of the tower. u = +20 m/s, a = −10 m/s², displacement on reaching the ground s = −25 m. Using s = ut + ½at²: −25 = 20t − 5t². Rearranging: 5t² − 20t − 25 = 0, i.e. t² − 4t − 5 = 0, so (t − 5)(t + 1) = 0. Rejecting the negative root, t = 5 s.
questions.explanation: Check: the ball rises for 2 s to 20 m above the top (45 m above ground), then falls 45 m in 3 s, giving 5 s in total.

questions.text: Passengers standing in a moving bus fall forward when the bus stops suddenly. This is due to:
questions.answer: Inertia of motion. The lower body stops with the bus, but the upper body tends to continue moving forward.
questions.explanation: A body in motion tends to remain in motion unless acted on by an external force.

questions.text: A force of 10 N acts on a body of mass 2 kg lying on a smooth surface. Find the acceleration produced in m/s².
questions.answer: From Newton's second law, F = ma, so a = F/m = 10 N / 2 kg = 5 m/s².

questions.text: A bullet of mass 20 g is fired horizontally with a velocity of 400 m/s from a gun of mass 4 kg that was initially at rest. Find the recoil speed of the gun in m/s.
questions.answer: Mass of bullet m = 20 g = 0.02 kg, v = 400 m/s; mass of gun M = 4 kg. Initial momentum = 0. By conservation of momentum: m v + M V = 0, so V = −(0.02 × 400)/4 = −8/4 = −2 m/s. The gun recoils with a speed of 2 m/s opposite to the bullet.
questions.explanation: The negative sign shows the gun moves opposite to the bullet.

questions.text: State Newton's third law of motion. Explain it with the help of two everyday examples.
questions.answer: Statement: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; action and reaction act on two different bodies at the same time. Examples (any two): (1) While walking, we push the ground backwards with our feet (action) and the ground pushes us forward (reaction). (2) When a swimmer pushes water backwards, the water pushes the swimmer forward. (3) When a gun is fired, the bullet moves forward and the gun recoils backwards. (4) A rocket pushes hot gases downwards/backwards and the gases push the rocket forward.

questions.text: (a) State Newton's law of gravitation. (b) Two bodies attract each other with a gravitational force F. If the mass of each body is doubled and the distance between them is also doubled, what is the new force? Show your reasoning. (c) Give two differences between mass and weight.
questions.answer: (a) Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = G m₁m₂ / r². [1 mark] (b) New force F' = G(2m₁)(2m₂)/(2r)² = 4Gm₁m₂/4r² = Gm₁m₂/r² = F. The force remains unchanged, equal to F. [1 mark] (c) Any two [2 marks]: Mass is the quantity of matter in a body, while weight is the force with which the Earth attracts the body. Mass is a scalar; weight is a vector. Mass stays the same everywhere; weight changes with the value of g. Mass is measured in kg with a beam balance; weight is measured in newton with a spring balance.

questions.text: The SI unit of pressure is the:
questions.answer: Pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
questions.explanation: Pressure is thrust per unit area, so its unit is N/m², named the pascal.

questions.text: A diver is at a depth of 20 m in a freshwater lake. The density of water is 1000 kg/m³, atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 10 m/s². Find (i) the pressure due to the water alone and (ii) the total pressure on the diver. Give the total pressure in pascal.
questions.answer: (i) Pressure due to water P = hρg = 20 × 1000 × 10 = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa. (ii) Total pressure = atmospheric pressure + hρg = 1.0 × 10⁵ + 2.0 × 10⁵ = 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa (300000 Pa).
questions.explanation: The atmosphere presses on the surface of the lake, and by Pascal's law this pressure is transmitted to every point in the water.

questions.text: In a hydraulic press, the area of the smaller piston is 10 cm² and that of the larger piston is 500 cm². A force of 20 N is applied on the smaller piston. Find the load that can be lifted by the larger piston, in newton.
questions.answer: By Pascal's law the pressure is transmitted equally: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂. So F₂ = F₁ × A₂/A₁ = 20 N × 500/10 = 20 × 50 = 1000 N.
questions.explanation: Areas can be used in cm² because only their ratio matters.

questions.text: Why is the wall of a dam made thicker at the bottom than at the top?
questions.answer: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth (P = hρg). The water at the bottom of the dam is deepest, so it exerts the greatest pressure on the wall there. The wall is made thicker at the bottom so that it can withstand this greater pressure.

questions.text: A body floats in a liquid when its weight is ____ the weight of the liquid displaced by its immersed part.
questions.answer: A floating body's weight is equal to the weight of the liquid displaced by its immersed part.

questions.text: A ship sailing from a river into the sea rises slightly higher in the water. This is because:
options: sea water is denser than river water
the weight of the ship decreases in the sea
sea water exerts less upthrust per unit volume
atmospheric pressure is lower over the sea
questions.answer: Sea water is denser than river water. A smaller volume of sea water has to be displaced to balance the same weight, so the ship floats higher.
questions.explanation: Upthrust = V × ρ × g; a larger ρ needs a smaller displaced volume V.

questions.text: A solid weighs 50 N in air and 30 N when fully immersed in water. Find the relative density of the solid.
questions.answer: Loss in weight in water = 50 − 30 = 20 N (this equals the weight of an equal volume of water). Relative density = weight in air / loss of weight in water = 50/20 = 2.5.
questions.explanation: Relative density has no unit because it is a ratio.

questions.text: A wooden block of volume 0.002 m³ and density 600 kg/m³ floats in water of density 1000 kg/m³. Taking g = 10 m/s², find (i) the weight of the block and (ii) the volume of the block that is under water. Give the submerged volume in cm³.
questions.answer: (i) Mass = volume × density = 0.002 × 600 = 1.2 kg; weight = 1.2 × 10 = 12 N. (ii) For floatation, upthrust = weight: V_sub × 1000 × 10 = 12, so V_sub = 12/10000 = 0.0012 m³ = 0.0012 × 10⁶ cm³ = 1200 cm³.
questions.explanation: Fraction submerged = density of block / density of water = 600/1000 = 0.6, and 0.6 × 2000 cm³ = 1200 cm³.

questions.text: (a) State Archimedes' principle. (b) Describe a simple experiment to verify it using a spring balance, a solid, an overflow (eureka) can and a beaker. (c) An iron nail sinks in water, but a ship made of iron floats. Explain why.
questions.answer: (a) When a body is wholly or partially immersed in a liquid, it experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of the liquid displaced by it. [1 mark] (b) [3 marks] Weigh the solid in air using the spring balance (W₁). Fill the eureka can with water up to its spout and place a weighed empty beaker (W₃) under the spout. Lower the solid, still hanging from the balance, until it is completely immersed; note the reading (W₂). Weigh the beaker with the overflowed water (W₄). Loss in weight = W₁ − W₂; weight of water displaced = W₄ − W₃. The two are found to be equal, which verifies Archimedes' principle. (c) [1 mark] The nail is solid, so the water it displaces weighs less than the nail and it sinks. A ship is hollow and shaped so that it displaces a very large volume of water; the weight of this displaced water equals the weight of the ship before it is fully submerged, so the ship floats.
questions.explanation: Floating depends on the average density of the body including the air inside, not just the material.

questions.text: Water has its maximum density at:
questions.answer: 4 °C. Water contracts on heating from 0 °C to 4 °C and expands above 4 °C, so its volume is least and density greatest at 4 °C.

questions.text: Gases such as carbon dioxide and methane, which trap infrared radiation in the atmosphere, are called ____ gases.
questions.answer: They are called greenhouse gases.

questions.text: (a) What is meant by the anomalous expansion of water? (b) Explain how this property helps fish and other aquatic animals survive in very cold weather. (c) State one other consequence of the anomalous expansion of water.
questions.answer: (a) When water is heated from 0 °C to 4 °C it contracts instead of expanding; above 4 °C it expands normally. This unusual behaviour is called anomalous expansion. [1 mark] (b) [2 marks] As the surface water of a pond cools to 4 °C it becomes densest and sinks, while warmer water rises. When the whole pond is at 4 °C, further cooling makes the surface water lighter, so it stays on top and freezes. Ice is a poor conductor of heat, so it insulates the water below, which stays at about 4 °C. Fish survive in this liquid water. (c) [1 mark] Any one: water pipes may burst in very cold regions because water expands on freezing; rocks crack when water in their crevices freezes (weathering).

questions.text: Give three differences between heat and temperature.
questions.answer: (1) Heat is a form of energy that flows from a hotter body to a colder body; temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body that decides the direction of heat flow. (2) The SI unit of heat is the joule (J); the SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K). (3) Heat is measured by a calorimeter (using the principle of mixtures); temperature is measured by a thermometer. Also accepted: the heat contained in a body depends on its mass, material and temperature, whereas temperature does not depend on mass.

questions.text: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror making an angle of 30° with the surface of the mirror. The angle of reflection is:
questions.answer: 60°. The angle of incidence is measured from the normal: i = 90° − 30° = 60°, and angle of reflection r = i = 60°.
questions.explanation: Angles of incidence and reflection are always measured from the normal, not the mirror surface.

questions.text: Two plane mirrors are inclined to each other at an angle of 60°. An object is placed between them. Find the number of images formed.
questions.explanation: The formula n = 360°/θ − 1 applies when 360°/θ is an even number.

questions.text: A girl stands 3 m in front of a plane mirror. She then walks 1 m towards the mirror. Find the new distance between the girl and her image in metres.
questions.answer: New distance of the girl from the mirror = 3 − 1 = 2 m. The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, i.e. 2 m. Distance between girl and image = 2 + 2 = 4 m.

questions.text: (a) State the two laws of reflection of light. (b) Give two characteristics of the image formed by a plane mirror. (c) State the relation between the focal length and the radius of curvature of a spherical mirror, and find the focal length of a concave mirror whose radius of curvature is 30 cm.
questions.answer: (a) [2 marks] (i) The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. (ii) The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. (b) [1 mark] Any two: the image is virtual and erect; it is of the same size as the object; it is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front; it is laterally inverted. (c) [1 mark] f = R/2. For R = 30 cm, f = 30/2 = 15 cm.

questions.text: Sound cannot travel through:
questions.answer: Vacuum. Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium to travel.
questions.explanation: In a vacuum there are no particles to vibrate and pass on the disturbance.

questions.text: Sound waves travelling through air are ____ waves, because the particles of air vibrate along the direction in which the wave travels.
questions.answer: Sound waves in air are longitudinal waves.

questions.text: A source produces sound of frequency 200 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m/s in air and 1480 m/s in water. Find the wavelength of the sound in air, and then find its wavelength when it travels in water. Give the wavelength in water in metres.
questions.answer: Using V = fλ. In air: λ = 340/200 = 1.7 m. The frequency is set by the source and does not change when sound enters water. In water: λ = 1480/200 = 7.4 m.
questions.explanation: When a wave passes into another medium, its speed and wavelength change but its frequency stays the same.

questions.text: During a thunderstorm, the flash of lightning is seen before the thunder is heard, although both are produced at the same time. Explain why.
questions.answer: Light travels at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s in air, while sound travels at only about 340 m/s. Since light is nearly a million times faster, the flash reaches us almost instantly, whereas the sound of thunder takes much longer to cover the same distance.

questions.text: The SI unit of electric charge is the:
questions.answer: Coulomb (C).
questions.explanation: The ampere is the unit of current, the volt of potential difference and the ohm of resistance.

questions.text: A charge of 30 C flows through a wire in 1 minute. Find the current in the wire in ampere.
A current of 0.2 A flows through a bulb connected across a 6 V battery for 5 minutes. Find the electrical energy consumed by the bulb in joule.
questions.answer: t = 5 min = 300 s. Charge Q = I t = 0.2 × 300 = 60 C. Energy W = V Q = 6 × 60 = 360 J (equivalently W = V I t = 6 × 0.2 × 300 = 360 J).

questions.text: (a) Define potential difference and state its SI unit. (b) Distinguish between conductors and insulators, giving two examples of each. (c) Why is copper commonly used for making connecting wires?
questions.answer: (a) [1 mark] The potential difference between two points is the work done in moving a unit positive charge from one point to the other (V = W/Q). SI unit: volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J/C. (b) [2 marks] Conductors allow electric current to pass through them easily because they have many free electrons, e.g. copper, aluminium, silver, iron. Insulators do not allow current to pass easily because they have almost no free electrons, e.g. rubber, glass, plastic, dry wood. (c) [1 mark] Copper has a very low resistance (it is a very good conductor), so little energy is wasted as heat; it is also ductile and relatively inexpensive.

questions.text: The surest test to find out whether a given iron bar is a magnet is:
options: attraction of iron filings at its middle
questions.answer: Repulsion with a known magnet. Attraction can happen between a magnet and any magnetic material, but repulsion happens only between like poles of two magnets.
questions.explanation: An unmagnetised iron bar is attracted by both poles of a magnet but is never repelled.

questions.text: Outside a bar magnet, magnetic field lines are directed from the ____ pole to the south pole.
questions.answer: Outside a magnet, field lines go from the north pole to the south pole.

questions.text: State three properties of magnetic field lines.
questions.answer: Any three: (1) Outside a magnet, field lines start from the north pole and end at the south pole; inside the magnet they run from south to north, forming closed curves. (2) Two field lines never intersect, because the field at a point can have only one direction. (3) Field lines are crowded where the field is strong (near the poles) and farther apart where it is weak. (4) The tangent to a field line at any point gives the direction of the magnetic field at that point.

questions.text: (a) What is induced magnetism? (b) What is a neutral point in the magnetic field of a bar magnet? (c) Why is soft iron, rather than steel, used as the core of an electromagnet? (d) State two ways of increasing the strength of an electromagnet.
questions.answer: (a) [1 mark] The temporary magnetism acquired by a magnetic material such as soft iron when it is placed near or in contact with a magnet is called induced magnetism. (b) [1 mark] A neutral point is a point where the magnetic field of the magnet is exactly balanced by the Earth's horizontal magnetic field, so the net field is zero and a compass needle placed there shows no particular direction. (c) [1 mark] Soft iron gets magnetised strongly and quickly when current flows and loses almost all its magnetism when the current is switched off, so the electromagnet can be turned on and off. Steel retains its magnetism. (d) [2 marks] Any two: increase the number of turns of the coil; increase the current in the coil; use a soft iron core (or bring the poles closer, as in a U-shaped core).
